summary.text: A 53-year-old Caucasian lifelong nonsmoking medical transcriptionist with no significant history presented after four months of exertional dyspnea and dry cough. Bilateral CT nodules were treated as presumed sarcoidosis with prednisone; subjective improvement after three months accompanied persistent CT nodules.

Core biopsy identified kappa-type amyloid and sarcoidosis was described as a misdiagnosis. CBC, kidney function, calcium, free light chains and urine protein were normal; urine M-protein and marrow clonal plasma cells were absent. Positive serum M-protein with mild IgG/kappa elevations led to localized lung AL amyloidosis and MGUS diagnoses. Prednisone was tapered off; no new treatment was initiated and actual outpatient pulmonology/oncology follow-up continued.

summary.text: A 63-year-old Caucasian man with prior hairy cell leukemia treated with chemotherapy and splenectomy in remission presented asymptomatically for enlarging bilateral pulmonary nodules. He had smoked 3–4 cigarettes weekly for ten years and worked as a skier. Nodules had been identified about ten years earlier, with VATS biopsy showing nodular amyloid degeneration four years earlier. Current nodules measured 3.8 × 4.3 cm in the right middle lobe and 2.8 cm retrocardiac.

Transbronchial biopsy showed lambda-type nodular amyloidosis; normal marrow and absent systemic involvement led to localized AL amyloidosis diagnosis and surveillance. After a few years, enlarging retroperitoneal nodes were excised at laparoscopy and showed EBV-positive nodular sclerosis Hodgkin lymphoma with focal hairy cell leukemia and negative Congo red. Brentuximab-vedotin, adriamycin, vinblastine and dacarbazine chemotherapy began, with ongoing clinic follow-up.

summary.text: A 74-year-old Asian nonsmoking accountant with calcified nodules under surveillance, past prolonged Legionnaire disease hospitalization, CPAP-treated OSA, hypertension and hyperlipidemia presented with hours of pleuritic pain and dyspnea. Vitals, CBC, CMP, troponin and D-dimer were normal and ECG showed no acute ischemia; chest x-ray showed left pneumothorax and collapse.

An 8-fr left anterior chest tube failed to resolve pneumothorax. CT showed a large loculated pneumothorax and calcified nodule, leading to VATS, left upper bullectomy, upper/lower wedge resections and talc pleurodesis. Incidental nodule biopsy revealed BALT marginal zone lymphoma and nodular amyloidosis with ossification without systemic amyloidosis. Subsequent chest CT stayed stable and oncology recommended no specific treatment.

Three years later an upper GI bleed attributed to NSAID/steroid use led to EGD diagnosis of gastric MALT lymphoma with negative H. pylori immunostaining. Oncology suggested no immediate treatment and continued surveillance; actual oncology and pulmonology follow-up remains ongoing.
